title: Why is a T-shirt cheaper than a sandwich?
teaches: One T-shirt's journey from Texas to China to Tanzania; trade quotas under the Multi Fibre Arrangement (1974 to 2004) and their end in 2005; Bangladesh's garment industry; fast fashion and short production cycles; Rana Plaza (2013); why sewing wages are a tiny part of a garment's price

blocks.text: In the late 1990s the economist Pietra Rivoli bought a white cotton T-shirt with a printed parrot for $5.99 from a bin in a Florida drugstore, and set out to find where it had come from. Her book, *The Travels of a T-Shirt in the Global Economy* (2005), followed it backwards and forwards around the world. Its cotton was grown on a family farm near Lubbock, Texas, on land worked with tractors, chemicals and government subsidies. The cotton was shipped to China, where it was spun into yarn, knitted into fabric and sewn into a shirt in a factory in Shanghai, by young women who had moved from the countryside. The shirt then went back across the Pacific to be printed and sold in Florida. When someone in the United States gave a shirt like it to charity, it was likely to be sold in a bale of used clothing to a trader in East Africa, where it was sold again in the second-hand markets of Tanzania.

In 1800 a shirt was an expensive possession. Today a basic T-shirt can cost less than a sandwich, and the average person in a rich country buys dozens of new garments a year. In this lesson we look at how clothing became so cheap, the trade rules that decided where it was made, and who bears the costs that the price does not show.
Lessons 3 and 12 used the hours bar to show where the work went in a sail and a length of chintz. The same arithmetic for a modern T-shirt shows how far the machines of this course have taken it.

blocks.caption: Rough estimates of the working time in one cotton T-shirt today, from mechanised cotton farming to a factory sewing line.

blocks.text: Every step except one is now done by machines that one worker tends in large numbers: cotton pickers, spinning frames, knitting machines and dye ranges. The exception is sewing. A sewing machine runs fast, but a person still has to guide every seam, because limp cloth is hard for machines to handle. That is why sewing is the largest share of the work in the bar, and why the garment industry has always moved to wherever sewing labour is cheapest, from the immigrant workshops of New York in lesson 24 to Hong Kong, China and Bangladesh.

From the 1950s, rich countries tried to protect their own textile and clothing industries from imports from Japan, Hong Kong, Taiwan and South Korea. In 1974 these arrangements were brought together in the **Multi Fibre Arrangement**, an international agreement under which importing countries such as the United States and the members of the European Community set **quotas**, fixed limits on how much of each kind of clothing each exporting country could send them every year.

The quotas had an effect no one intended. Once an exporter such as Hong Kong had used up its quota, its manufacturers looked for countries that had quota to spare and set up factories there. Clothing production spread to dozens of poor countries, from Sri Lanka and Mauritius to Bangladesh and Cambodia, not because they were the cheapest places to sew but because they still had quota. In Bangladesh, according to the usual account, the industry began in 1978 when a former civil servant, Noorul Quader, formed a partnership with the South Korean firm Daewoo, which needed quota. Daewoo trained 130 Bangladeshi workers in its factory in Busan, and most of them later left to start garment firms of their own.

Under a World Trade Organization agreement of 1995 the quotas were phased out over ten years, and the last ended on **1 January 2005**. Buyers could now order from wherever was cheapest, and China's exports of clothing to the United States and Europe rose so fast in 2005 that both imposed temporary limits again. Bangladesh, with even lower wages, kept growing. It is now the world's second largest exporter of clothing after China. Garments make up more than four fifths of its exports, and its factories employ about four million people, most of them women.

Cheap production changed how clothes are sold. A traditional clothing firm designed its collections a year ahead and ordered them in large batches. The Spanish firm Inditex, owner of Zara, built a different system from the 1980s: small first batches, close watch on what sold in its shops each day, and factories near Spain that could make more of the popular designs and deliver them to shops within a few weeks. Unsold lines were dropped quickly. This **short cycle** meant fewer unsold clothes and more new designs in the shops, and customers learned to visit more often. Other firms copied it, and online sellers such as Shein have since shortened the cycle further, adding thousands of new designs a day.

blocks.caption: Prices in the United States: all consumer goods and services against clothing, 1990 to 2023, with 1990 as 100. Rounded, from the Bureau of Labor Statistics consumer price index.

blocks.text: Over these three decades the general level of prices in the United States more than doubled, while clothing prices barely moved, so clothing became less than half as expensive compared with everything else. Global clothing production roughly doubled between 2000 and 2014, according to an estimate by the Ellen MacArthur Foundation, while the average number of times a garment was worn before being thrown away fell by about a third.

On 23 April 2013, large cracks appeared in the walls of Rana Plaza, an eight-storey building in Savar, on the edge of Dhaka. It held shops and a bank on its lower floors and five garment factories above. The shops and the bank closed. The next morning, factory managers ordered their workers back inside, and some were told they would lose their pay if they refused. Shortly before 9 am on **24 April**, when the power failed and the factories' generators started, the building collapsed. 1,134 people were killed and about 2,500 were injured, most of them garment workers. The upper floors had been added without permission, and the building had not been designed for heavy machinery.

Labels from many European and American brands were found in the rubble. Within weeks, more than 200 brands and retailers, most of them European, signed the **Accord on Fire and Building Safety in Bangladesh** with global unions, a legally binding agreement to pay for independent inspections and repairs in the factories that supplied them. A group of North American firms set up a separate, non-binding Alliance. Inspectors found safety hazards in almost every factory they visited, and thousands of repairs were made. Bangladesh's government also raised the minimum wage for garment workers, though it remains among the lowest in the world.

The people who sew a garment receive a very small part of what it sells for. Researchers and campaigners have published many breakdowns of clothing prices, and they agree on the shape: most of the price goes to the shop and the brand, which pay for rent, staff, advertising, design, unsold stock and profit. Cloth, transport and duties take most of the rest. The factory's own costs and profit are a few percent, and the wages of the sewers are often under 1 percent.

blocks.caption: A rounded breakdown of a €29 branded T-shirt, after published breakdowns. Cheaper shirts have different shares, but sewing wages stay a small part.
blocks.task: Triple the sewers' wages and compare the two ways of passing on the cost

blocks.text: In the figure, tripling the wages of the people who sew the shirt raises its shop price by a few percent at most. This calculation is why campaigners argue that higher pay is affordable. It leaves out several things. Factories compete fiercely for orders, so one that raises its wages alone may lose its customers to another factory or another country, and buyers often push for lower prices each season. Higher wages could also speed up the replacement of sewers by machines, which is starting in some factories. Whether a pay rise sticks therefore depends on whether brands, governments and unions apply it across a whole industry, as the Accord did for building safety.

items.ask: Why is sewing still the largest share of the work in a modern T-shirt?
choices: Limp cloth is hard for machines to handle, so a person still guides every seam
Sewing machines are slower than hand sewing
Cotton must be sewn before it is spun
Laws require garments to be sewn by hand
items.why: Spinning, knitting and dyeing are run by machines one worker tends in large numbers. Sewing still needs a person at each machine.

items.ask: How did the quotas of the Multi Fibre Arrangement help start garment industries in countries such as Bangladesh?
choices: Exporters that used up their own quota set up factories in countries with quota to spare
They banned clothing made in China
They paid poor countries to build factories
They set a minimum wage for garment workers
items.why: Quotas limited each country's exports, so production spread to countries that still had room under their limits.

items.ask: What happened when the last quotas ended on 1 January 2005?
choices: Buyers moved orders to the cheapest producers, and China's exports jumped
Clothing prices rose sharply
Bangladesh's garment industry closed
Production moved back to the United States
items.why: Without quotas, buyers could order wherever was cheapest. China grew fastest, and Bangladesh, with lower wages, also kept growing.

items.ask: What made Zara's short cycle different from a traditional clothing firm?
choices: Small first batches, daily sales data and nearby factories that could restock popular designs within weeks
Larger orders placed a year ahead
Selling only online
Making every garment by hand
items.why: The short cycle cut unsold stock and put new designs in shops often, which brought customers back more often.

items.ask: In the figure, tripling sewing wages raises a €29 shirt's price by a few percent at most. What does that calculation leave out?
choices: Factories compete for orders, so one that pays more alone may lose its buyers
Wages are most of the price
Brands pay sewers directly
Shirts are priced by weight
items.why: The arithmetic shows a pay rise is small next to the price. Competition between factories and countries is what makes a rise hard for one factory to make alone.

summary: **A T-shirt crosses the world.** Rivoli's shirt was grown in Texas, made in China, sold in Florida and resold in Tanzania.
**Sewing is the last hand step.** Every other stage is tended by machines; a person still guides every seam.
**Quotas spread the industry.** From 1974 the Multi Fibre Arrangement limited each country's exports, so production moved to countries with quota to spare.
**The quotas ended in 2005.** Orders moved to the cheapest producers, above all China and Bangladesh.
**Fast fashion shortened the cycle.** Small batches, sales data and quick restocking put new designs in shops every few weeks.
**Clothing got relatively cheaper.** US clothing prices barely changed from 1990 to 2023 while prices overall more than doubled.
**Rana Plaza killed 1,134 people.** The 2013 collapse led to a binding safety accord between brands and unions.
**Sewers get a tiny share.** Wages are often under 1 percent of the price, but competition makes a raise hard for one factory alone.
